newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ trade data seen consistent with cooling economy.
newsitem.headline: NZ trade data seen consistent with cooling economy.

text.p: New Zealand merchandise trade data on Thursday was consistent with a picture of a cooling economy, economists said.
Statistics New Zealand (SNZ) said the trade balance was in deficit to the value of NZ$2 million in March, against economists' expectations of a $183 million surplus.
The year to March data was also worse than expected, with an annual deficit of $498 million, against economists' average forecast of a $258 million deficit.
However, dealers said the trade series was notoriously volatile and the financial market reaction had been minimal.

The surprise March deficit was counterbalanced in part by a $27 million surplus for the March quarter, up from a deficit of $215 million in the previous quarter and against a $6 million deficit in the March 1996 quarter.
ANZ Bank economist Bernard Hodgetts said the quarterly data was not an indication of a healthy export picture.

"Okay, it's a little bit improved on a year ago, but it seems to me that much of that improvement is really coming about because of the drop in imports. That I suppose is associated with the economy cooling off, and business investment in particular slowing down," he told Reuters.
Bancorp Treasury Services said in a commentary the import trend could be an area of concern.
"This is not promising for the Reserve Bank, as it needs greater import penetration at times of high exchange rates, in order to push dopwn domestic prices," it said,
ANZ's Hodgetts noted that exports for the March quarter, worth $4.88 billion, were down from a year ago ($5 billion).
"It's a mirror of the investment picture from GDP. It really does confirm that the economy is in a bit of a fragile state on the external side," he added.
Exports were worth $5.22 billion in the December quarter.
Hodgetts noted that the exports trend remained negative.
ASB Bank economist Anthony Byett said exports could be volatile as they were dependent to a large degree on the actions of major commodity producers.
"The imports were the one that surprised me, because everything else we're seeing at the moment is suggesting the economy is starting to slow down," he said.
Imports fell to a value of $4.85 billion in the March quarter, from $5.43 billion in the previous quarter and $5 billion in the March 1996 quarter.
He agreed with Hodgetts that the falling imports were largely responsible for the quarter trade balance improvement.
"Nonetheless it has to be acknowledged that exports are staying up near the levels of last year in spite of a somewhat higher Trade-Weighted Index," he said.
